title: The Sharing Trial

pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 7: Fairness is a number everyone can see.*

Dawn broke over the Terrace Plains in a wash of pale yellow, illuminating a standoff that had been brewing since the previous night. Two hundred villagers from the upper and lower slopes stood on either side of the narrow, sputtering stream, their faces tight with hunger and suspicion. They did not look at the water. They looked at Wen.

The pressure of their gazes was a physical thing, pressing against her chest, squeezing the air from her lungs. She felt the familiar, unwelcome surge of power rising in her fingertips, a cold itch that promised relief if she simply reached out and grabbed the flow. It would be so easy. She could lift the water, twist it, and pour it exactly where they wanted. But the ledger in her mind, the quiet voice of her mother’s almanac, warned her: *to take is to owe.*

"Choose," shouted a man from the lower terrace, his voice cracking with desperation. "Give us the water, Bearer. We have children who have not eaten in two days."

"Give it to us," countered a woman from the upper slope, stepping forward with a stick in her hand. "Our fields are higher. If we fail, the whole slope washes away. We have the right to the source."

Wen closed her eyes. The crowd began to chant her name, a low, rhythmic hum that vibrated in the soles of her boots. It sounded like worship, but it felt like a noose. They were not asking for help; they were demanding a verdict. They wanted her to be a god, to decide who lived and who starved, to take the burden of their choice onto her shoulders.

Her hand trembled. The white frost streak at her left temple seemed to burn in the morning light. She hated this. She hated that her gift was being treated as a coin to be spent, a tool to be used. She was not a dispenser of mercy. She was a girl who could move water, and the cost of that movement was written in the ice on her skin.

"I will not choose," she said, her voice thin but steady.

The chanting stopped abruptly. The silence that followed was heavier than the noise. Two hundred pairs of eyes fixed on her, waiting for the other shoe to drop, for the magic to save them or the cold to kill her.
pages.image: Two large groups of villagers in straw hats and simple clothes stand on opposite banks of a narrow, shallow stream, pointing and shouting at a small figure in the center, Wen, who stands with her hands clasped tightly at her sides, her expression tense and defiant, terraced fields rising steeply behind them in the dawn light.

pages.text:
Wen turned to the only person in the crowd who was holding a map instead of a stick. Shen Yu was already moving, his round glasses catching the sun as he hurried to the stream’s edge. He looked terrified, but his hands were steady as he unrolled a length of hemp rope.

"Measure," Wen said, her voice shaking only slightly. "If we know how much there is, we know who can have it. And when."

Shen Yu nodded, his eyes wide behind the brass rims. He tied one end of the rope to a smooth stone and waded into the knee-deep water, his grey cloth shoes instantly soaking through. He held the rope taut across the stream, marking the width with a notch on the bark of a nearby willow. Then he took a single dry leaf, dropped it into the current, and started counting.

"Three seconds," he called out, wiping his face with an ink-stained sleeve. "The flow is slow. Sluggish. It is like moving syrup."

Wen watched the leaf drift. It took four seconds to pass the second marker. The water was barely moving, a thin ribbon over a bed of loose gravel. She looked at the terraces, the dry, cracked mouths of the fields waiting for a drink. There was not enough water to fill them all at once. There was not enough water to fill them all today.

"But," Shen Yu said, his voice gaining confidence as he scribbled figures on a scrap of paper, "if we restrict the flow, if we turn it on for only one field at a time, and for a set amount of time, we can stretch it. We can make it last for a week."

Wen looked at the old stone gate, the one with the strange, jagged notches cut into its frame. It was not a dam. It was a mechanism. A clock.

"The notches," she said, pointing to the stone. "They are not decorative."

Shen Yu blinked, then looked closely at the gate. "They are measurements," he whispered. "Centimeters. Millimeters. Someone built this to meter the flow. To share it."

The crowd murmured. The anger in their faces softened into confusion, then curiosity. They had been fighting over a prize, but they had not looked closely at the prize.
pages.image: Shen Yu wading in a shallow, rocky stream, holding a taut rope across the water, a single dry leaf floating nearby, Wen watching intently from the bank, her hand resting on her hip, the stone gate with jagged notches visible in the background, the terraced fields empty and dry.

pages.text:
They spent the next hour in a frenzy of calculation. Shen Yu’s hands moved quickly over his map, drawing lines and shapes, while Wen watched the water, feeling its pulse against her skin. She could sense the depth, the pressure, the tiny amount of friction as the water slid over the stones. It was a delicate thing, this stream, a vein rather than a river.

"We have to be exact," Shen Yu said, his voice tight with concentration. "If we open the gate too wide, the water will rush to the lowest field and leave the upper ones dry. If we open it too little, the silt will clog the channel."

Wen knelt beside the gate. The notches were worn smooth by centuries of use. She ran her finger over them, feeling the grooves. Each notch represented a specific amount of water, a specific time. It was a language of fairness, written in stone.

"Turn the gate to the third notch," Wen said. "For the lower fields first. They are the most vulnerable. Then the middle. Then the top."

Shen Yu hesitated. "But the upper villagers will be last. They will be angry."

"They are thirsty," Wen said. "But they are not dying. The lower fields have no backup. The upper fields have the forest above them. We have to prioritize the desperate, not the loud."

The crowd listened. The man who had shouted earlier lowered his stick. The woman from the upper slope crossed her arms, but she did not argue. She was watching the water, watching the notches, watching the logic of it.

The river did not care who you were. It only cared about the slope, the volume, the time. And for the first time in three days, the air in the valley felt less like a battlefield and more like a workshop.
pages.image: Wen kneeling beside a stone water gate with visible notches, her hand tracing the grooves, Shen Yu holding a map and a stick, pointing to a section of the stream, the crowd standing in the background, their expressions shifting from anger to attentive listening, the dry terraces stretching up the hillside.

pages.text:
The problem was that the gate was stuck. Decades of silt and algae had packed into the hinge, freezing the stone wheel in place. It was a small clog, but it was enough to stop the flow.

Wen stepped forward. The crowd parted, not in reverence, but in anticipation. She placed her palm on the wet stone of the gate. The cold bit into her skin, familiar and sharp. She did not lift the water. She did not move the stone. She simply pressed her palm against the clog, feeling the trapped sludge, and pushed.

It was a small move. A tiny amount of force. But it was enough to break the seal. The gate groaned, then turned.

A surge of water, no larger than a bucket, rushed out. It hit the first channel, splashing against the dry earth. The sound was small, but it was the sound of life.

The lower villagers cheered. It was not a roar of triumph, but a soft, collective exhale, the sound of a held breath finally released.

Tianzhu stepped forward. He did not speak. He simply reached into his pocket and pulled out his straw hat. He placed it gently on Wen’s head, shading her from the brightening sun.

"Little bearer," he said, his voice rough with emotion. "You did not give them water. You gave them a share."

Wen touched the hat, feeling the texture of the straw. She looked at her hand. The frost was still there, but it felt lighter. Less like a debt, and more like a tool.

The gate ran by itself now, the water flowing in a steady, measured stream. The village did not need a hero. It needed a schedule. And for the first time, Wen realized that she was not the one keeping the river alive. The river was keeping the village alive, and she was just the one holding the door open.
pages.image: Wen standing with a straw hat on her head, her hand resting on the turned stone gate, a small, steady stream of water flowing from the gate into a channel, Tianzhu standing beside her with a gentle smile, the lower villagers in the background looking relieved and hopeful, the terraced fields beginning to show signs of moisture.

pages.text:
Master Gao stood on the bank, his polished black boots untouched by the mud that coated the villagers’ feet. He watched the water flow with a face of polite interest, while the rest of the crowd celebrated with the rough joy of people who had just remembered how to breathe. He did not cheer or shout. He simply observed, his eyes tracking the stream as a merchant tracks a price.

"Remarkable," he said, his voice smooth and uninflected. "You have solved a problem that has plagued this valley for a generation. With such... efficiency."

Wen looked at him, her hands still stained with the dark silt of the gate hinge. "We just started," she said. "There are still two hundred fields to feed."

Gao smiled. It was a charming smile, the kind that made you want to trust him, but it did not reach his eyes. "You are young, and you are tired," he said. "The road to the source is long. The water is further up. If you stay here, fixing every gate, every clog, you will never reach the headwaters. You will become a local fixer, not a Bearer."

He leaned in, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper that cut through the noise of the returning farmers. "Leave them to their schedule. It works. Go. The source is waiting. And the true answer is there."

Wen looked at the villagers, who were already gathering their tools, moving to their fields. They were busy, and they were alive. They did not need her to save them; they needed her to leave.

But as she turned to go, she saw Gao’s face. He was not disappointed. He was relieved. His shoulders dropped a fraction as the pressure of her presence lifted from the air.

She looked down at her mother’s map, the one tucked into her pack. In the margin, in small, careful letters, she wrote: *Gao wants her to leave. Why?*

The wind shifted, carrying the scent of wet earth and growing rice. The valley was healing. And somewhere, upstream, the river was still silent.
pages.image: Master Gao standing on the bank, smiling politely, his hands clasped behind his back, Wen looking at him with a wary expression, her hand resting on her map case, the villagers in the background working in their fields, the water gate flowing steadily in the distance, the sun casting long shadows across the terraces.
